description: We’re Team SN, passionate about AI, computer vision, space, and remote sensing. We’re building SatQuery AI, a multimodal satellite imagery assistant. Looking for people interested in AI/ML, GIS, data science, web development, space science, or research. If you like building and solving real-world problems, join us!
summary: What is changing, where, and how strong is the evidence? LavaLabs turns 42 years of NASA Earth data into an investigation anyone can replay. Choose air temperature or annual precipitation, compare regional model cells, and see the direction, rate, and statistical significance of each trend. At the cell matched to Syapru Besi, Nepal, annual precipitation rose by 177.2 mm per decade from 1984 to 2025, while the temperature trend remained inconclusive. Then open the saved August 2026 flood. Switch from radar to optical RGB, see which communities and crossings were flagged for verification, and download the evidence behind the priorities. LavaLabs gives students, analysts, and response planners a way to decide which changes warrant a closer look and where to verify conditions on the ground.
details:
Is it getting wetter near Syapru Besi?

Open Nepal Investigation, choose Annual precipitation, and select the Syapru cell. LavaLabs draws the annual series, shows the fitted rate, and lets you compare the result with neighboring model cells. At the cell matched to Syapru Besi, the 1984–2025 precipitation trend is +177.2 mm per decade (95% interval +114.4 to +240.1, Holm-adjusted p = 0.0000262). Switch to air temperature and the verdict changes. Its +0.041 °C per decade estimate is inconclusive. A rising line and a statistically supported trend have different implications for what to investigate next.

How the trend detective works

NASA POWER provides monthly temperature and precipitation from MERRA-2. We convert the monthly values to annual series, retain 42 complete years for each of 15 regional grid cells, and estimate the rate of change per decade. We account for time dependence with HAC uncertainty estimates and adjust across 30 cell–variable comparisons. The interface shows location, magnitude, and significance together. Download the annual CSV, original NASA values, and a JSON record of the selected result to check the calculation.

Does the result survive a different fit?

We apply the calendar-month climatology, anomaly and ordinary/robust comparison approach from Acker et al. (2009), a NASA study listed in this challenge’s resources. Switch between the seasonal cycle and annual departures, compare ordinary and Huber robust fits, and export all 504 monthly departures. For Syapru rainfall, the slopes are +177.2 and +177.6 mm per decade: little sensitivity to this fitting choice. The primary significance test remains separate. The receipt names the paper, its source hash and our adaptation, making the method inspectable as well as the result.

From a regional trend to a local field check

Open the saved 26 August 2026 flood and switch the response map to Optical RGB. The long NASA record gives regional context. The dated Sentinel-1 observations, matching Sentinel-2 RGB, and historical OpenStreetMap layers show where to focus local checks.

  • Priority 1 — Check people. Review two mapped structures that intersect radar water candidates and check in with nearby mapped communities, including Pajung and Syapru Besi.
  • Priority 2 — Verify access. Inspect the two flagged crossings before assigning transport and check road and destination status locally.
  • Priority 3 — Recheck coverage gaps. Ask for ground reports where radar missed the surface. Each pin shows the reason it was flagged, and the briefing export preserves the underlying evidence.

The response workflow ranks field-verification tasks from historical observations. It leaves road access unknown where the available network or observations cannot resolve it.

What we built and what the case studies add

LavaLabs brings the statistical investigation, local event review, and evidence downloads into one public workspace. The four prior SATQuery research cases show why the choice of evidence matters. Syapru Besi illustrates steep-valley flood and access questions. Kedarnath shows how clouds limit a historical Landsat comparison. Varanasi examines riverfront land-cover change, and Sangam Vihar illustrates dense urban drainage and terrain-scale limits. Our research manuscript in preparation studies how comparing vegetation change (NDVI), optical and radar scenes, and terrain can qualify what a satellite signal supports.

We built the challenge workflow and public integration using Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, JavaScript, and Plotly.js. The prior SATQuery flood engine, terrain and NDVI tools, and four case studies are credited in the repository. The free public site packages the saved runs so reviewers can replay the investigation immediately. OpenAI Codex assisted code, analysis and verification, visual design, and writing. SI-generated artwork is identified in the interface.
